~20% is absorbed in the stomach, the rest in the small intestine; 90–98% is oxidized in the liver, 2–10% is excreted unchanged through the lungs, urine and sweat

Department textbook and Kharkevich: ethyl alcohol
Below are the main points from the Department of Pharmacology's teaching material and D.A. Kharkevich's textbook. Green blocks show differences from modern recommendations.
A colorless, highly flammable, light liquid with a characteristic smell.
In medicine it is used mainly as an antiseptic and a solvent; because it is widely consumed in beverages, its resorptive action must be known.
It has a general depressant (narcotic-type) effect on the CNS.
40% — dilates skin vessels and causes hyperemia (irritant, warming compress).
70% — the most effective for skin antisepsis: it penetrates the deep layers of the epidermis.
95–96% — rapidly coagulates proteins, giving an astringent effect; disinfection of cutting instruments.
For hand antisepsis the WHO recommends 60–80% alcohol-based products; 96% alcohol penetrates poorly and is less effective.
A small dose weakens inhibition in the cortex — "false excitation": critical thinking decreases, emotion increases.
First analgesia, then a long period of excitation, then the "surgical" stage — consciousness is lost.
The narcotic margin is very narrow: the surgical stage quickly passes into the agonal stage (paralysis of the respiratory and circulatory centers). For this reason ethanol is not used for anesthesia.
Skin vessels dilate — heat loss increases and body temperature falls (risk of rapid freezing in the cold).
Suppresses the secretion of antidiuretic hormone — diuresis increases.
Stomach: concentrations up to 20% increase secretion; higher concentrations reduce HCl and pepsin production and cause pylorospasm.
1 g of ethanol provides 7.1 kcal, but the energy is not stored; alcohol cannot be a nutrient or plastic material.
Treatment: gastric lavage, oxygen, in severe cases hemodialysis and symptomatic therapy.

The analeptics mentioned in the textbook are no longer recommended. The main measures are to secure the airway, place the patient on the side, thiamine, then glucose, infusion and warming. Gastric lavage only within 1 hour of drinking and if the airway is protected.
Mental work, memory and thinking decline; Korsakoff psychosis, alcoholic delirium (delirium tremens).
Polyneuritis, chronic gastritis, hepatitis, cirrhosis, fatty degeneration of the heart and kidneys.
Functional cumulation: even when ethanol is not detected in the blood, changes in the CNS keep accumulating.

There is an unmeasured osmotically active substance in the blood: methanol, ethylene glycol, isopropanol or acetone. With anion-gap metabolic acidosis and visual disturbance — methanol; with kidney injury and oxalate crystals — ethylene glycol. Decide on fomepizole (or ethanol) and hemodialysis.

An unconscious young man found on the street
A 22-year-old man was brought in by his friends: he drank a lot of vodka at a party. Strong smell of alcohol, traces of vomit around the mouth, responds weakly to sound and pain.
Clear the airway, place on the side, give oxygen
Correct. In an unconscious intoxicated patient the main cause of death is aspiration of vomit and respiratory depression. Start with ABC.
It is not proven that a benzodiazepine was taken; flumazenil can provoke seizures and does not act on ethanol.
In an unconscious patient with an unprotected airway, gastric lavage leads to aspiration. Ethanol is absorbed quickly — lavage has little benefit.
Analeptics are not recommended in modern practice: the effect is short and they cause seizures.
Glucose 2.8 mmol/L. What do you do?
Correct. In a patient who has been drinking, glucose without thiamine can trigger Wernicke encephalopathy. The hypoglycemia is due to excess NADH — gluconeogenesis is inhibited.
Hypoglycemia must be corrected, but if glucose is given without thiamine there is a risk of Wernicke's. Thiamine first (or at the same time).
Insulin in hypoglycemia is wrong and dangerous.
Observe, it will recover on its own
Hypoglycemia damages the brain — correct it immediately.
Warm infusion (0.9% NaCl), warming, monitoring, protection from vomiting
Correct. Hypotension is due to vasodilation and dehydration, hypothermia to heat loss. The patient is in intensive care or an observation ward, protected from aspiration.
Fluids first; vasopressors are ineffective in hypovolemia.
A diuretic increases dehydration; it hardly speeds up ethanol elimination.
Sobering agents do not speed up ethanol metabolism.
The patient regained consciousness after 8 hours. Blood ethanol had been 3.6 ‰. Before discharge: brief advice on alcohol consumption (AUDIT), and an explanation of the risks to relatives.
A 45-year-old man drank cheap alcohol bought at the market. After 18 hours his vision became blurred ("as if it were snowing"), with abdominal pain and deep, noisy breathing.
Correct. A latent period + visual disturbance + anion-gap and osmolar-gap metabolic acidosis — the classic signs of methanol (formic acid).
There is no ethanol in the blood; ethanol does not cause such severe acidosis and visual disturbance.
There is no information about glucose; visual disturbance and an osmolar gap are not typical of DKA.
Ethylene glycol also causes acidosis and an osmolar gap, but its main sign is kidney injury and oxalate crystals, not vision.
Fomepizole (if unavailable — ethanol intravenously or by mouth)
Correct. Both occupy ADH and stop the formation of formaldehyde and formic acid from methanol. The target ethanol level is ≈ 1–1.5 ‰.
What is needed besides the antidote?
Correct. Hemodialysis removes methanol and formic acid (indicated in severe acidosis and visual disturbance), bicarbonate reduces acidosis, folic acid speeds up the breakdown of formic acid.
Methanol poisoning leads to blindness and death — active treatment is needed.
After 18 hours the methanol has already been absorbed.
Fomepizole and hemodialysis were started. Vision partly recovered. The sanitary service was notified to find other people who drank from the same batch — group poisonings are common.

Correct. 48–96 hours after drinking stops: confusion, visual hallucinations, autonomic hyperactivity (fever, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating). Also rule out fat embolism and infection.
Confusion and autonomic signs are typical of delirium, not psychosis.
There is a fever, but the clinical picture and timing fit withdrawal; sepsis is ruled out, but the main diagnosis is delirium.
An important differential after a femoral fracture, but the hallucinations and history point to delirium.
Correct. Benzodiazepines substitute for ethanol through GABA<sub>A</sub>, reducing seizures and death.
It lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat the cause of delirium; only as an add-on to benzodiazepines.
It increases respiratory depression and does not treat delirium.
Thiamine IV in a high dose, fluids, restore K⁺ and Mg²⁺, monitoring
Correct. In alcoholic delirium the risk of dehydration, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and Wernicke's is high.
Restraint only temporarily; without sedation it is dangerous (rhabdomyolysis, aspiration).
Naltrexone is for the long-term treatment of dependence, not for acute delirium.

With diazepam and thiamine the delirium resolved in 3 days. Later a consultation with an addiction specialist was arranged and a plan was made to treat the dependence with naltrexone or acamprosate. Prevention: when an alcohol-drinking patient is admitted, monitor with CIWA-Ar and give prophylactic thiamine.

A 48-year-old man who has been drinking heavily for 15 years and eats poorly. For 2 days he has been confused and staggers when walking, with bilateral nystagmus, and cannot move his eyeballs sideways.
Correct. The classic triad: ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus), ataxia, confusion. The cause is thiamine deficiency; the triad does not have to be complete.
Blood ethanol is low; the signs do not fit drinking.
Symmetric eye-movement disturbance and the history point to Wernicke's; it is excluded with CT/MRI.
There is no asterixis or signs of liver failure; ophthalmoplegia is not typical.
Thiamine 500 mg IV three times a day for 3–5 days
Correct. High-dose parenteral thiamine, then oral. Magnesium is also checked (needed for the effect of thiamine).
B₁₂ deficiency gives a different clinical picture (funicular myelosis).
The reverse order — glucose consumes thiamine and makes the condition worse.
Untreated, mortality is ~20% and the risk of progression to Korsakoff's is high.
Korsakoff syndrome: anterograde amnesia and confabulation
Correct. The mammillary bodies and thalamus are damaged — memory is impaired irreversibly.
Two days after thiamine, eye movements recovered and the ataxia decreased, but the memory impairment partly persisted. Conclusion: thiamine prophylaxis for every patient with alcoholism.
Metronidazole and a glass of wine

A 30-year-old woman is taking metronidazole for trichomoniasis. She drank a glass of wine at a birthday party; 15 minutes later her face flushed, her heart is beating fast, she has a headache and feels nauseous.
ALDH inhibition — accumulation of acetaldehyde (disulfiram-like reaction)
Correct. Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase; acetaldehyde causes vasodilation, tachycardia and nausea.
No urticaria, bronchospasm or swelling; the timing in relation to drinking points to a disulfiram-like reaction.
No clonus or hyperreflexia, no serotonergic drugs.
The clinical picture does not fit.
Lay down, fluids, symptomatic treatment; in severe cases oxygen and monitoring
Correct. The reaction usually passes within a few hours; infusion for severe hypotension.
Not needed unless there are signs of anaphylaxis.
Which other drugs give such a reaction with alcohol?
Correct. The patient is told not to drink alcohol during treatment and for 48–72 hours after it ends.
They do not cause a disulfiram-like reaction.
The reaction passed in 3 hours. Conclusion: when prescribing metronidazole, tell the patient not to drink alcohol both verbally and in the prescription's signature line.

Through which sequence of enzymes is ethanol mainly broken down?
Alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde, and aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2) oxidizes it to acetic acid.
What kinetics does ethanol elimination follow?
ADH becomes saturated at low concentrations — a constant amount per unit of time (≈ 7–10 g/h; ≈ 0.15 ‰/h) is broken down.
A 70 kg man drank 63 g of ethanol (r = 0.68). What is C<sub>max</sub> by Widmark?
How many grams of pure ethanol are in 500 ml of beer (5%)?
A = 500 × 0.05 × 0.789 ≈ 19.7 g ≈ 20 g — about 2 standard drinks.
How many per mille is "300–400 mg%" in the department textbook?
100 mg% = 1 g/L = 1 ‰, so 300–400 mg% = 3–4 ‰ — acute poisoning.
Why is the concentration higher in a woman at the same weight and dose?
The fraction of body water (r) is smaller
The Widmark coefficient is the fraction of body water: man 0.68, woman 0.55. Smaller r → larger C.
The most effective ethanol concentration for skin antisepsis:
70% (60–80%) alcohol, together with water, denatures proteins better and penetrates; 96% coagulates at the surface and does not penetrate deeper.
In thiamine deficiency transketolase and pyruvate dehydrogenase do not work. The triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion.
What is given before glucose to an intoxicated, unconscious patient?
Glucose without thiamine can trigger Wernicke encephalopathy.
A laboratory sign typical of alcoholic hepatitis:
In alcoholic injury AST is two or more times higher than ALT; GGT also rises.
The first-choice drug in alcohol withdrawal and delirium:
Benzodiazepines substitute for ethanol through GABA<sub>A</sub> and prevent seizures.
Which drug causes a disulfiram-like reaction when alcohol is drunk?
Metronidazole (also tinidazole, cefoperazone) inhibits ALDH — acetaldehyde accumulates.
Fomepizole (or ethanol) occupies ADH and stops the formation of formaldehyde and formic acid.
Osmolar gap 30, anion-gap acidosis, visual disturbance — the most likely cause:
Visual disturbance + acidosis + osmolar gap — methanol. Isopropanol gives ketosis without acidosis.
The mechanism of action of disulfiram (Teturam):
ALDH is inhibited and acetaldehyde accumulates — flushing, vomiting and tachycardia when alcohol is drunk; a conditioned-reflex aversion develops.
